parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Start by recalling what a normal single X-ray shows and why it is limited - all the structures along the beam overlap into one flat shadow.
Hint 2: Think how you could get more 3D information about just one thin cross-section or slice through the body instead of the whole thickness.
Hint 3: Consider why taking just one view of that slice is not enough, and what rotating the X-ray tube and detector around the patient would add.
Hint 4: Think about what must be done with all those different-angle views to turn them into a clear picture of that one slice.
Hint 5: Now extend the idea - how do you go from one slice to a full volume image of an organ or the whole body?
parts.proper_answer: X-ray images are taken through a thin slice/section of the patient from many different directions/angles. A computer processes these to produce a 2D image of that slice. This is repeated for many slices along the patient to build up a 3D image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why a normal X-ray is not enough**
Think of a chest X-ray as a shadow. All the bone, muscle and organs that the beam passes through overlap on the film. You cannot tell depth. CT solves this by looking at just one thin slice at a time.

Step 2: **Many views of the same slice**
In CT, a narrow X-ray beam and detectors rotate around the patient. They take many images of that same slice from different directions and angles all the way round, typically through 360 degrees. Each view records how much the X-rays are attenuated by the tissues along that line.

Step 3: **Computer builds the 2D slice image**
The computer combines all these angular attenuation data to calculate the attenuation at each small point in the slice. It then produces a detailed 2D cross-sectional image of that slice.

Step 4: **Repeat for many slices**
The patient is moved slightly along and the process is repeated for the next adjacent slice. This is done for many slices along the length of the region being examined.

Step 5: **Stack to make a 3D image**
All the 2D slice images are then stacked together by the computer to build up a complete 3D image of the object or patient, which can be viewed from any angle.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: need for fast processing and large storage
hints: Hint 1: Look back at your answer to (a) - how many separate images must be stored and mathematically combined to make just one slice image?
parts.proper_answer: Combining the many views to form each slice image involves complex processing/subtraction of images, requiring fast processing and large memory.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Huge amount of data to handle**
You have just seen that each slice needs images from many angles, and a full scan needs many slices. The computer must store all this data and perform subtraction and reconstruction calculations very quickly. That was only possible once fast computers with large memories became available.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: radiation dose and number of exposures
hints: Hint 1: Compare the number of X-ray exposures in a single leg-bone radiograph with the number needed for a full CT scan described in (a).
parts.proper_answer: A CT scan consists of very many slices/images, each requiring X-ray exposure, whereas a leg X-ray is a single image, so total dose is much larger.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Dose adds up with every image**
An X-ray of a leg bone is essentially one quick exposure. A CT scan takes many views per slice and many slices per scan, so the patient is exposed many, many times. Total radiation dose is the sum of all these exposures, so it is much larger.
